newsitem.title: USA: Dollar gains on strong U.S. data, weak German mark.
newsitem.headline: Dollar gains on strong U.S. data, weak German mark.

text.p: The dollar rose broadly Friday, setting a near 31-month high against the German mark, as strong overseas trade and manufacturing data highlighted a vigorous U.S. economy.

Also aiding the dollar was further weakness in the mark against most other European currencies. Over the past week, the mark not only sank to its lowest level against the dollar since June 1994, but hit more than four-year troughs against the British pound and the Norwegian and Danish crowns.
A lackluster German economy and expected bumpy ride toward European monetary convergence contrast sharply with current U.S. monetary stability and economic vitality, traders said.

"The trade and manufacturing numbers showed the United States economy is pulling ahead of Europe's. It is a natural pulling apart and is largely responsible for the dollar's drive higher," said Gabriel Grippo, chief dealer at Credit Agricole in New York.

The Commerce Department said record U.S. exports held growth in the November trade deficit to 4.9 percent as the shortfall between exports and imports rose to $8.4 billion, well below an anticipated larger deficit figure.

In a separate report, the Federal Reserve said national industrial output grew a surprisingly strong 0.8 percent in December, the same as in November, as businesses operated at their fastest rates in more than a year.

The dollar peaked at 1.6190 marks in late trading after Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin repeated his assertion, stated twice earlier this week, that a strong dollar is in the United States' interest and "will remain so".
His remark quashed market speculation that the Clinton administration was opposed to the dollar's new, lofty heights.
However, concerns lingered that Japanese monetary authorities may intervene in the foreign exchange markets to support the ailing yen.
Reported comments by an unidentified source close to Japan's Ministry of Finance, saying Japan was unwilling to sell dollars, failed to dispel those fears, dealers said.
The dollar rose to 117.37 yen from 116.54 at Thursday's close, buoyed by the report that showed the United States' November trade deficit with Japan shrank 12.9 percent to $4.32 billion.

The dollar closed at 1.6182 German marks, a significant jump from Thursday's 1.5945 close. The dollar also touched a new 32-month high against the Swiss franc at 1.40 before closing at 1.3993 Swiss francs, up from 1.3767 on Thursday.

Highlighting German economic woes, a newspaper report Friday said the government was increasingly concerned it would overshoot the strict budget deficit criteria needed to qualify for European economic and monetary union.
The Bonn Finance Ministry quickly retorted that the German government still expected to meet the criteria.

But the Handelsblatt newspaper, quoting unidentified officials, said a public spending freeze would be imposed this month and that Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt assumed there would be 4.2 million jobless in Germany in 1997 -- 200,000 above the previous target.
In other trading, the dollar fell to Canadian $1.3405 from C$1.3413 at the end of trading Thursday. Sterling fell to $1.6672 from $1.6795.
